prompt:
You are a rigorous analyst working for a technology watch team.

DECISION QUESTION:
D'ici 12 mois, une entreprise de services numériques peut-elle s'appuyer sur les résultats des benchmarks d'agents LLM (SWE-bench, WebArena, etc.) pour confier des tâches de développement de routine à des agents autonomes, ou ces scores surestiment-ils leur fiabilité réelle, ce qui impose de se limiter à des expérimentations contrôlées ?

SUB-QUESTIONS:
- SQ1: Que mesurent réellement les benchmarks d'agents, et quelles sont leurs limites (contamination des données, tâches peu réalistes) ?
- SQ2: Quel écart observe-t-on entre scores publiés, évaluations indépendantes et retours d'expérience réels ?
- SQ3: Quelles approches d'agents (planification, mémoire, outils, multi-agents) sont réellement matures ?
- SQ4: Quels échecs et risques sont documentés (fiabilité, injection de prompt, actions destructrices) ?
- SQ5: Où les affirmations des fournisseurs divergent-elles des sources indépendantes ?

TASK: read the DOCUMENT below and extract at most 5 claims that help answer the decision question.
If the document is not useful for the question, return [].

RULES (mandatory):
1. "citation": copy ONE passage VERBATIM from the document: the exact same characters, 1 or 2 consecutive
   sentences, between 30 and 300 characters. Never paraphrase, never translate, never merge separate passages,
   never use "...". If you cannot quote a passage that supports the claim, do not output the claim.
2. "texte": the claim restated in FRENCH, in one sentence, faithful to the citation, adding nothing.
3. "categorie", one of:
   - "fait": verifiable fact or measured result
   - "interpretation": opinion, analysis or conclusion of the author
   - "lacune": missing evidence, unknown, limitation of what has been measured
   - "risque": documented failure, incident or risk
   - "signal": weak signal or emerging trend
4. "theme", one of:
   - "performance_benchmark": scores and results reported on agent benchmarks (SWE-bench, WebArena...)
   - "validite_benchmark": what benchmarks really measure: contamination, realism, flawed tests, gaming
   - "usage_reel": results in real-world use, production deployments, field feedback, productivity
   - "fiabilite_securite": failures, errors, destructive actions, prompt injection, security and safety
   - "maturite_approches": maturity of agent techniques: planning, memory, tool use, multi-agent
   - "supervision_humaine": need for human review, oversight, controlled pilots, governance
5. "position" with respect to the question:
   - "optimiste": supports that agents / benchmark scores are reliable enough for routine development tasks
   - "critique": suggests scores overestimate real reliability, or documents failures, risks or limits
   - "neutre": neither
6. "sous_question": "SQ1" to "SQ5", or null.

Answer with JSON only: a list of objects with keys "texte", "citation", "categorie", "theme", "position", "sous_question".

Source: METR (independant), published 2026-05-19

"""
Assessment Window: Feb 16, 2026 – Mar 16, 2026 Download PDF Redaction summary statement: Except where explicitly noted in the report, there was no additional redacted information that was important to our conclusions from any of the participating companies. Executive summary and guide to the report Starting in February 2026, METR conducted a pilot exercise to assess misalignment risks from AI agents used inside frontier AI developers, with participation from Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI. We make three main contributions in this report, each detailed in a separate section. First, we motivate and outline the process we followed for this exercise. 1 Each participant provided: Access to their most capable internal model(s) at the time of assessment, including raw chains of thought. A wide range of non-public information about the capabilities of the shared model(s), how AI was used and monitored internally, and trends in the pace of progress. METR then prepared private reports for each participant, participants approved what non-public information could be disclosed, and METR wrote this public report. This exercise is entity-based rather than model-specific, and is designed to be repeated periodically rather than tied to public releases. Second, we present six key facts that inform our assessment, drawing on evaluations we conducted on the models that participants shared, 2 evaluations we conducted on public models, information shared by participants, 3 findings from a recent embedded red-teaming exercise , 4 system cards, and other public literature. We organize facts into means (what harmful actions agents could take), motive (whether they might attempt harmful actions) and opportunity (whether attempts could succeed, given safeguards). Finally, we provide an assessment of whether internal AI agents in Feb–Mar 2026 had the means, motive , and opportunity to start a “ rogue deployment ” — a set of agents running autonomously without human knowledge or permission — and make it robust against varying degrees of security and monitoring measures. Overall, we believe that internal agents at the time of our assessment plausibly had the means , motive , and opportunity to start small rogue deployments, but they did not have the means to make them highly robust. All sources All models Incidents With risk regions Public materials METR evaluations Shared by companies ? Hypothetical Download incidents chart (PNG) Download incidents chart with risk regions (PNG) Download incidents.json Explore the incidents chart on its own page Given rapidly advancing capabilities, we expect the plausible robustness of rogue deployments to increase substantially in the coming months. We tentatively plan to run a similar process in late 2026. We’re grateful to Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI for participating in a process that involved more direct access to non-public information and more editorial independence than in previous external evaluation engagements. 5 We’re especially grateful to the staff at each company who put substantial effort into iterating with us on a process with no established template and many moving parts. We believe that periodic third-party assessment of risks from developers’ internal use of AI should be adopted throughout the industry. Pilot process To date, third-party evaluations of frontier AI have largely focused on evaluating individual models for dangerous capabilities before they are deployed to the public, but standard pre-deployment evaluations have important limitations. They generally capture no information about training and safeguards, and often leave little time for thorough analysis given fast-paced launch schedules. Most importantly, third-party evaluations triggered by public deployments are not designed to cover risks from internal use within the developer itself. In early February 2026, METR initiated a pilot of an alternative format: an entity-based (not model-specific) assessment of risks from internal use of AI within AI developers, which is designed to be repeated periodically (not tied to public launches). Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI participated in this pilot. The exercise had four phases: Figure 1: Overview of the frontier risk report process and information flows. Information gathering (late February through mid-March 2026). Each participant provided: Access to their model(s), including raw chains of thought. METR asked participants to share the model that represented their internal state of the art at the start of the assessment. 6 Responses to a detailed questionnaire we prepared, which asked for information about the capabilities and propensities of the shared model(s), how AI was used and monitored internally, and trends in the pace of progress. Evaluations and private reports (early March through early April 2026). METR produced a company-specific private report for each participant, typically with evaluation results on the shared models, an analysis of their questionnaire answers, and tentative high-level recommendations. 7 Disclosure approval (April 2026). METR drafted lists of attributed and non-attributed key claims relating to each company pulled from its respective private report, and selected any transcripts that needed company approval. Each participant exercised its rights to redact or anonymize these before approving them for inclusion in this public report. 8 Importantly, at any point before approving their final materials, participants could exit silently , meaning we would treat them as if they had never participated. This means that any company could have withdrawn partway through the process for any reason, and we would not note this anywhere. Industry-level report (late April through mid-May 2026). METR wrote this report, incorporating publication-approved materials from participating companies and our evaluation results 9 . Participants received a draft approximately one week before publication but did not have approval rights over this final report. Figure 2: Categories of information from private reports, grouped by whether companies could redact before inclusion in the industry-level report. In addition to evidence generated specifically through this exercise, this report is heavily informed by public evidence. We believe that capability gaps between internal and public models have been small for the most prominent developers in recent years, based on a mix of public reporting, our general engagement with the industry, and the argument that companies face commercial pressure to publicly deploy state-of-the-art systems ahead of competitors. This pilot lets us give somewhat more direct assurance for participating companies: All participants (Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI) stated that the model(s) they shared represented their internal state-of-the-art at some point in the mid-February to mid-March 2026 assessment window. Our evidence indicates that none of the models shared with us were significantly more capable than the models with the strongest publicly documented capabilities as of May 19, 2026. Evidence source Public frontier (Feb–Mar 2026) Internal frontier (Feb–Mar 2026) Time horizon 1.1 50% ~12h [5h-61h] Likely* ≥16h, internal frontier on average ~2 months ahead of public frontier Time horizon 1.1 80% ~1.5h [50m-2h40m] Likely* ≥3h but <4h Early version of MirrorCode Mostly saturated, >100h time horizon N/A, due to saturation from public models Subversion Strategy Eval** 72% ≤80% No-CoT Math ~4m <10m Challenge tasks One edge-case success, seven clear failures One edge-case success, seven clear failures; more progress on some tasks * The TH 1.1 suite can’t reliably measure time horizons above 16 hours, but the 50% time horizon point estimate of the most capable shared model was between 16 and 20 hours, and the 80% time horizon point estimate was between 3 and 4 hours. **We only evaluated a subset of Subversion Strategy Eval due to refusals. Table 1: There was a modest gap between the internal and public frontier in Feb–Mar 2026 on the evaluations we conducted, though saturation issues make our conclusions highly uncertain. None of the models shared with us were significantly more capable than the models with the strongest publicly documented capabilities as of May 19, 2026. For details see Table E.1 of Appendix E . We cannot provide assurance about internally deployed models for non-participating companies. However, we are not aware of credible public reporting 10 suggesting that internally deployed models at non-participating companies are substantially more capable than the most capable models publicly documented to date. As such, we believe that the strongest publicly documented capabilities as of May 19, 2026 are likely representative of the strongest capabilities across the industry at the time of our assessment. Company Available sources of evidence Amazon Recent model cards, technical reports and service cards , general access to public models Anthropic Evaluations from this exercise , Claims from this exercise , recent system cards & risk reports , METR’s embedded red-teaming exercise of Anthropic monitors, general access to public models Google Evaluations from this exercise , Claims from this exercise , recent system cards , general access to public models Meta Evaluations from this exercise , Claims from this exercise , the recent safety & preparedness report , general access to public models Microsoft Recent model cards and technical reports , general access to public models OpenAI Evaluations from this exercise , Claims from this exercise , recent system cards and details about monitoring , general access to public models xAI General access to public models Table 2: Sources of evidence available for this exercise, drawn from Frontier Model Forum member companies and xAI. We describe the pilot process (model access guidelines, questionnaire, redaction and anonymization policy, and silent exit options) in more detail in Appendix A . We tentatively plan to run a similar process later in 2026. Key facts In this section, we give an overview of the core evidence that informs our assessment. We focus on the risk of misaligned AI agents intentionally taking harmful actions. 11 We organize our findings into six “key facts,” grouped into three factors: Means : What types of harmful actions did these agents have the capabilities, access, and tools to carry out? Motive : Given their propensities and incentives, what types of harmful actions might these agents have attempted, and under what circumstances? Opportunity : Given safeguards like security and monitoring, what harmful actions could these agents have carried out without being detected and stopped? Figure 3: Overview of the key facts that inform our assessment. These facts are relevant for understanding a wide range of harms that misaligned internal agents could plausibly cause; the Risk assessment section discusses whether assessed agents plausibly had the means , motive , and opportunity to create rogue deployments and make them robust against human intervention. Means Coding agents did real projects that would take humans hours or days Benchmarks. The most capable agents we evaluated essentially saturated our Time Horizon 1.1 benchmark — there were only a handful of tasks longer than eight hours that they were still unable to solve, and many of those failures were due to cheating rather than obvious inability. 12 Their measured time horizon was over two full-time-equivalent days, though we are increasingly uncertain about the point estimate due to saturation. Agents displayed even stronger capabilities on an early version of MirrorCode , a software reimplementation benchmark we developed with Epoch AI — the most capable agents we evaluated were able to solve tasks that would take humans weeks. 13 Figure 4: We find that public models in Feb–Mar 2026 had several times longer time horizons on the software reimplementation tasks in MirrorCode-Early than they did on the broader Time Horizon 1.1 suite. While we have limited data, the doubling time seems similar or slightly faster. The MirrorCode agents had different token limits, which could lead to overestimating the doubling time, see details in Appendix E . Other popular software, ML, mathematics, and cybersecurity benchmarks seemed to paint a broadly similar picture, though this is hard to assess precisely. Many benchmarks were saturated or seemed near saturation, 14 and scores on unsaturated benchmarks might have been much higher if agents were given inference budgets comparable to what it would cost to hire a human. Benchmarks generally lacked measured human completion times, but our guess, based on rough impressions of task difficulty, is that most benchmarks had very few tasks that would take a human multiple full-time-equivalent days or longer. Public anecdotes. Consistent with our MirrorCode results, publicly reported anecdotes indicate that agents were exceptionally strong on problems that are easily “hill-climbable” — those where progress is cheap to verify and many approaches can be tried cheaply — including software reimplementation (as in MirrorCode), many optimization problems, some areas of mathematics, some forms of debugging, and some forms of vulnerability discovery. For example, Claude Mythos Preview nearly autonomously discovered thousands of vulnerabilities across several pieces of commercial software including Firefox and Linux, and Opus 4.6 nearly autonomously built a limited 15 C compiler ; we believe these tasks would take weeks or months for a human expert to do on their own. Challenge tasks. To probe the limits of these strengths, we ran agents on three “challenge” problems that were more open-ended than benchmark tasks but that seemed relatively hill-climbable: Pen-testing METR’s evaluation infrastructure. We asked agents to hack our scoring system, escape their sandboxes, or modify METR codebases. Given a budget of $500-$5000 (see Table 3), one of the most capable shared models discovered and exploited a JavaScript injection vulnerability in the Inspect viewer , a widely used tool for viewing agent transcripts. In theory, the vulnerability could have let it arbitrarily alter displayed transcripts and scores displayed on that page — although as we discuss in the next section , it only succeeded in carrying out one very limited exploit. It also identified a few other vulnerabilities in our infrastructure. Building a custom version of dvc . We asked agents to build a customized version of an open source data version control library, with specific improvements targeted at METR’s workflows — a project that had recently taken a METR engineer several weeks of work. With a budget of several thousand dollars, Opus 4.6 made progress equivalent to perhaps a few days of work by a METR engineer, although its implementation had issues. 16 Finding vulnerabilities in runc . reponse.texte: Les agents les plus avancés ont saturé le benchmark Time Horizon 1.1, et nombre de leurs échecs sur les tâches de plus de huit heures étaient dus à des comportements de triche plutôt qu'à une incapacité manifeste.
reponse.citation: The most capable agents we evaluated essentially saturated our Time Horizon 1.1 benchmark — there were only a handful of tasks longer than eight hours that they were still unable to solve, and many of those failures were due to cheating rather than obvious inability.

reponse.texte: La plupart des benchmarks d'agents ne mesurent pas les temps de résolution humains et comportent très peu de tâches exigeant plusieurs jours de travail humain.
reponse.citation: Benchmarks generally lacked measured human completion times, but our guess, based on rough impressions of task difficulty, is that most benchmarks had very few tasks that would take a human multiple full-time-equivalent days or longer.

reponse.texte: Sur un projet d'ingénierie réel doté d'un budget de plusieurs milliers de dollars, le modèle Opus 4.6 n'a produit que l'équivalent de quelques jours de travail humain et son code comportait des anomalies.
reponse.citation: With a budget of several thousand dollars, Opus 4.6 made progress equivalent to perhaps a few days of work by a METR engineer, although its implementation had issues.

reponse.texte: METR estime que les agents internes disposaient vraisemblablement des moyens, de la motivation et de l'opportunité pour initier de petits déploiements autonomes non autorisés, même s'ils ne pouvaient pas encore les pérenniser solidement.
reponse.citation: Overall, we believe that internal agents at the time of our assessment plausibly had the means , motive , and opportunity to start small rogue deployments, but they did not have the means to make them highly robust.
